alternatives.argument: At p, take the global harmonic conjugate of g_p on X minus p, correct its -2pi pole period, and exponentiate to a holomorphic f_p:X->D with a simple zero at p and |f_p|=exp(-g_p). At q compose f_p with a disc automorphism sending f_p(q) to zero. Leastness bounds g_q above by minus its log modulus. At p, symmetry of Green kernels makes this inequality an equality. On the complement of q and the other zeros of the transformed map, the nonnegative difference is harmonic and attains its minimum zero at p. This complement is connected because a discrete subset does not disconnect a surface; the strong maximum principle makes the difference zero throughout, and extension across the deleted zeros shows there were no other zeros and the zero at q was simple. Thus f_p is injective. Its image is a simply connected proper plane domain, so the published Riemann mapping theorem gives a biholomorphism of the image with D. Full AC enters through that theorem; the surface Green and symmetry suppliers require only Countable Choice.

First, a nonconstant bounded holomorphic h would give a finite upper bound on each compact-support Green competitor v by applying the maximum principle to v+(1+epsilon)log|B(h)|, where B sends h(p) to zero; the Green dichotomy forbids it. Exponentiate the dipole complexification, using the +1 and -1 integral periods, to obtain a meromorphic map F:X->sphere with one simple zero p and one simple pole q. For any r use the dipole with zero r and pole q to get F_r; the quotient (F-F(r))/F_r is holomorphic and bounded outside the pole discs, hence globally bounded and therefore constant on a nonGreen surface. It is nonzero by evaluating at p or q, so F takes the value F(r) only at r. Thus F is injective. If its simply connected image omitted two sphere points, a Möbius change would put it in a proper simply connected plane domain and the Riemann mapping theorem would yield a nonconstant bounded holomorphic function, contradiction. Hence the image omits at most one point; compactness distinguishes sphere from plane. Full AC is inherited from Riemann mapping.

Fix p and form the canonical surface Green envelope. Its dichotomy is finite or infinite. In the finite case the Green-function branch supplies a biholomorphism to D. In the infinite case the dipole branch supplies a biholomorphism to C or the sphere according to compactness. The model inequivalence lemma gives uniqueness. Both branches use abstract-surface Green/Dirichlet arguments; the earlier plane-domain mapping theorem is invoked only after the new Green map embeds the surface into C. AC enters through the two branch lemmas’ calls to the published Riemann mapping theorem, while countable choices enter the exhaustion and normal-family construction.
